title: Quality evaluation of stroke-related information on TikTok: a cross-sectional study
screen_reason: Cross-sectional content analysis of the 100 most-liked English-language stroke videos on TikTok (January 2025). Besides the quality instruments, the authors coded each video for 'any inaccurate information' and report 31/100 (31.0%) plus concrete falsity subcategories (unproven treatments promoted 12%, incorrect symptom information 8%, misleading prevention claims 7%, dangerous home remedies 4%, delayed care recommendations 3%). That is an explicit falsity coding of items with a stated denominator, i.e. CONTENT; the GQS/mDISCERN/VIQI/PEMAT/JAMA instruments give additional QUALITY rows.

estimates.country: Not stated for the videos; collection account configured as located in the United States, English-language videos only
estimates.date: Data collection 15-20 January 2025 (coding reported as 8-18 January 2025)
estimates.measure_type: % of the 100 most-liked stroke-related TikTok videos containing any inaccurate information (misinformation)
estimates.value_raw: Any inaccurate information, n (%): 31 (31.0) of All Videos (n=100)
estimates.denominator: 100 TikTok videos: the most-liked results of searches on #stroke, #strokeawareness, #strokeprevention, #strokesymptoms and #strokerecovery, English-language, 15 s to 10 min, with a primary focus on stroke health information (160 identified, 20 duplicates removed, 40 excluded)
estimates.definition: the video was coded as containing inaccurate information in at least one of six categories: unproven treatments promoted, incorrect symptom information, misleading prevention claims, dangerous home remedies, delayed care recommendations, or (for healthcare professionals) oversimplified explanations
estimates.misinfo_def: No formal definition is given. The operational categories in Table 4 are "Any inaccurate information", "Unproven treatments promoted", "Incorrect symptom information", "Misleading prevention claims", "Dangerous home remedies", "Delayed care recommendations"
estimates.source_quote: Misinformation appeared in 31% of videos, with significant variation by creator type
estimates.page_loc: Results, 'Misinformation Analysis'; Table 4 row 'Any inaccurate information, n (%)': All Videos (n=100) 31 (31.0), HCP 3 (8.8), content creators 19 (42.2), general users 9 (42.9), p<0.001
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two authors independently assessed each video, with a third arbitrator settling disagreements; inter-rater reliability reported as Cohen's kappa = 0.78 ("substantial"), stated for the video QUALITY assessments. No separate rubric, guideline benchmark or reliability figure is reported for the misinformation/accuracy coding itself, and no external fact-check or guideline document is cited as the standard.
estimates.moderator_quote: A systematic search of the TikTok platform was conducted ... using a comprehensive set of stroke-related hashtags, including #stroke, #strokeawareness, #strokeprevention, #strokesymptoms, and #strokerecovery. To capture content with the highest user engagement and visibility, results were filtered using the platform's "most-liked" function.
estimates.notes: CONTENT rather than QUALITY because the numerator is an explicit falsity judgement (incorrect symptom information, unproven treatments, misleading prevention claims, dangerous home remedies), not a completeness/usefulness score - a wholly accurate video could not attract the label. Confidence is medium because the accuracy coding procedure is undocumented (the reported kappa = 0.78 attaches to the quality instruments) and no external ground-truth document is named. denom_selection=curated: 'most-liked' rank-truncated hashtag sample. Two date inconsistencies in the paper: data collection is given as 15-20 January 2025 but the two raters are said to have coded 'from January 8 to 18, 2025', i.e. before collection ended. Country is coded Global/unspecified because only the collecting account was US-located and only English-language videos were kept; an adjudicator could defensibly code United States. The verbatim source_quote is limited to the narrative sentence because the PDF interleaves 'ACCEPTED ARTICLE IN PRESS' watermark fragments inside the following clause and because Table 4's cells are split across lines ('Any inaccurate 31 (31.0) 3 (8.8) 19 (42.2) 9 (42.9) <0.001 information, n (%)' in reading order).

estimates.country: Not stated for the videos; collection account configured as located in the United States, English-language videos only
estimates.measure_type: % of the 100 most-liked stroke videos scoring 3 or above on the Global Quality Score (i.e. at least moderate overall quality)
estimates.value_raw: Global Quality Score (GQS) Score >=3, n (%): 43 (43.0) of All Videos (n=100); mean GQS 2.68 +/- 0.89
estimates.denominator: the same 100 most-liked stroke-related TikTok videos
estimates.definition: video scored 3 or higher on the 5-point Global Quality Score (1 = poor to 5 = excellent) for overall quality of stroke-related content
estimates.misinfo_def: n/a - GQS measures overall educational quality, not veracity
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two independent raters plus arbitrator, Cohen's kappa = 0.78; GQS is a validated 5-point global quality scale.
estimates.moderator_quote: The GQS13, a 5-point scale, assessed overall video quality of stroke-related content, ranging from poor (1) to excellent (5).
estimates.notes: QUALITY row, excluded from prevalence per the instructions. POLARITY WARNING: 43% is the share scoring AT OR ABOVE the quality threshold (good quality), not the share of low-quality videos; the low-quality share (57%) would be a computed complement and is therefore not recorded (R8). Only one of the paper's four threshold-based quality shares is recorded here to avoid inflating the row count; the others are listed in missed_or_uncertain.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) Creator-type subgroups of the 31% misinformation figure were not given their own rows (they are subgroups of the same 100 videos): healthcare professionals 3/34 (8.8%), content creators 19/45 (42.2%), general users 9/21 (42.9%), p<0.001. They are prominent in the abstract, so an adjudicator may want them. (2) Sub-categories of the 31% are nested numerators over the same denominator and would double-count: unproven treatments promoted 12 (12.0%), incorrect symptom information 8 (8.0%), misleading prevention claims 7 (7.0%), dangerous home remedies 4 (4.0%), delayed care recommendations 3 (3.0%). (3) Other threshold-based QUALITY shares not written as rows: mDISCERN >=3 52 (52.0%); VIQI total >=15 ('high quality') 38 (38.0%); PEMAT understandability >=70% 74 (74.0%). Instrument means (GQS 2.68+/-0.89, mDISCERN 2.56+/-1.02, VIQI 12.4+/-3.2, PEMAT-U 75.8+/-15.4%, PEMAT-A 65.2+/-23.8%) are means only and per the instructions generate no row. (4) Content-coverage shares (only 23% addressed prevention, 67% symptom recognition, 31% treatment information, 42% evidence-based information, 19% referenced guidelines) are topic-coverage/completeness measures, not falsity, and were not extracted. (5) Creator composition (HCPs 34%, content creators 45%, general users 21%) and verification rates are sample descriptors. (6) The 'up to 80% of strokes are preventable' figure is a clinical statistic cited from elsewhere. (7) The text file is an accepted-manuscript proof: the words 'ACCEPTED ARTICLE IN PRESS' and stray letter columns are interleaved throughout, sometimes mid-sentence; all values above were nonetheless recoverable verbatim from the narrative and from Tables 2 and 4.

rob.design: Cross-sectional analysis of 100 TikTok videos, collected 15-20 January 2025 from a newly created, history-free account configured as a 25-year-old US user (to limit algorithmic personalisation), searching five stroke hashtags and taking the platform's 'most-liked' results; 160 identified, 20 duplicates removed, 40 excluded (irrelevant 15, personal narrative 12, out-of-duration 8, non-English 5). No probability sample and no sampling of less-viewed content, so the estimate is for popular content only. Two authors coded independently with a third arbitrator; Cohen's kappa = 0.78 for the quality assessments. Instruments: PEMAT, VIQI, GQS, JAMA, mDISCERN. Misinformation coding is reported as a set of six accuracy categories but with no stated rubric, no external guideline benchmark and no separate reliability statistic. Non-parametric group comparisons (Mann-Whitney, Kruskal-Wallis), Spearman correlations, SPSS 29.
rob.item6_quote: Misinformation appeared in 31% of videos, with significant variation by creator type (Table 4). ... The most problematic categories included: unproven treatments (12% of all videos, exclusively from non-professionals), incorrect symptom information (8%), and misleading prevention advice (7%).
